title: Underkeep is my favorite old-school dungeon crawler since Legend of Grimrock, and yes that includes Queen's Domain
summary: Queen's Domain might be the trendy game of the moment but for my money, the classic grid-based action of Underkeep is where it's at. (And yes, there's a demo.)
body: Everyone's talking about Queen's Domain right now, but as someone who tried Queen's Domain and did not care for it, allow me to direct your attention to an alternative old-school dungeon crawler: Underkeep, which launched on Steam on November 5 and has been absolutely phenomenal through the roughly four hours I've put into it so far. Like Queen's Domain, Underkeep is firmly rooted in the 1990s, but I'm talkin' the early '90s, and even before that: Classic grid-based RPGs like The Bard's Tale, Dungeon Master, Wizardry, and Eye of the Beholder. In fact, as someone who loves Eye of the Beholder (specifically the second one, The Legend of Darkmoon), I noticed a lot of nearly direct lifts from that series: primarily visual, but also a few audio cues, that I swear I've heard before. title: All that stands between a hacker and admin privileges on some Linux distros is a 257-character long string of literally anything
summary: Eeeeeeeeeeeeeep. Thankfully there's already a fix out.
body: Some implementations of secure shell (SSH), one of Linux's most trusted and secure connection protocols, have been found vulnerable to the most peculiarly simple methods of bypass: spamming characters. On some distros, simply type 257–1,024 characters and you get access to the root (admin) login. Thankfully, the list of vulnerable distros is quite small and niche, and OpenSSH has already issued a workaround/fix. In some new release notes , OpenSSH explains that "this release contains a critical security workaround that affects Linux systems that use the musl libc and PAM disabled." "Sshd(8): avoid password authentication bypass that is exploitable through sshd(8) that affects some Linux systems when built and run with PAM support disabled. We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside sshd, but it is exploitable via sshd and can be avoided there." SSH itself is a longstanding and ubiquitous networking protocol that anyone who has dabbled even lightly in Linux networking projects will be familiar with. title: Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR review
summary: Mid-range, mighty, and mini.
body: It feels like every new bit of tech in a gaming keyboard or gaming mouse is treated as the next frontier, from new switch types to higher polling rates, and even the materials used. But if you want 8,000 Hz polling, it actually does feel like TMR might be the next frontier, because not only is it snappy and responsive, but it's super efficient, which helps counteract some of the problems with high polling in the first place. Right now, the pickings are fairly slim for TMR keyboards. We've got some from Logitech , some from Cherry , and a few others , but it's still a relatively niche sensor technology for switches right now, and not exactly cheap. But TMR is great, and it's particularly good if you want to go wireless thanks to its power efficiency. Epomaker's HE75 V2 TMR is interesting partly because it crams that switch technology into an 8,000 Hz board with a ton of little quality-of-life features, and does it all at a price point amongst the cheapest TMR keyboards. title: WoW: Forever takes 250,000 GB of memory to run, and I can't even joke about Sam Altman being jealous because that's almost nothing compared to the monolithic demands of AI
summary: That's a lotta gigs.
body: MMOs are kinda costly to run, but as it turns out, nowhere near as costly as a datacenter. I was going to spend most of this article joking about how Sam Altman, who doesn't like that we have RAM , would be frothing at the mouth for that kind of compute power. After a bit of research I am leaving horrified at the sheer industrial heft the AI industry requires. The numbers were revealed by the official WoW X account , which states that WoW Forever runs on about 3,924 virtual machines, 251,136 GB of memory, and 70,480 CPU cores. To give you an idea of how much server infrastructure that is, our best budget CPU goes for around $110 at the moment, and it has six cores. Fudge the maths a bit and that's $1.2 million in cores alone. Which is pricey, don't get me wrong—though not perhaps for a company that has hundreds of thousands of players paying a sub each month. body: Ultima creator Richard Garriott was one of several developers on a recent panel hosted by the Georgia Game Developers Association, and Lord British was in fine form. Calling himself the "great-grandpa" of the group, he began by summarizing the current problems faced by the videogame industry. "It's not just one thing," Garriott began. "I think if it was one thing it would be a lot easier to diagnose and come back from, but it's a lot of folks who don't understand videogames trying to make money off of videogames, it's a political climate, it's a billion things. title: Critical Role's upcoming series with Hololive gave Matt Mercer 'a deeper understanding and appreciation' for vtubers
summary: Shattered Legends is a six-episode miniseries that will debut later this month.
body: Neither Critical Role diehards nor Hololive vtuber fans could've predicted that they'd work together to film a new tabletop roleplaying series. Shattered Legends is the product of a collaboration that might sound bizarre at first but makes perfect sense when you consider vtubers are basically just voice actors, like just about everyone else in Critical Role's orbit. Matt Mercer certainly sees them that way. He tells PC Gamer that filming Shattered Legends with Hololive vtubers gave him a "deeper understanding and appreciation for the skill and talent that each of these performers has." title: Nexus Mods takes the Valve approach to AI-generated content: No outright bans but mandatory disclosures

body: Nexus Mods, the world's largest mod site and more or less a second home for anyone who's ever installed a Bethesda game, has new rules regarding AI-generated and AI-assisted mods on its platform. In short, it's taking a Steam-ish approach: no outright bans on AI content, but it's compulsory to disclose where it's been used in your mods, and to what extent. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use", wrote Nexus owner Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann in an update yesterday. "We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform". So, starting yesterday, modders uploading new projects to Nexus will have to tick a box declaring how much AI was used in their work, including promotional materials. They can declare their mods "AI-generated", which is to say mostly produced by AI; "AI assisted", for mods that are mostly human-made with a little LLM assistance on the side; or declare them free of the tech's touch altogether.
